description: Hand-labeled evaluation set for the 7 seeded incident docs (server/seed/*.md). Documents are labeled by file_name (unique in the DB, stable across re-seeds). Chunk indexes are as produced by the current chunker (maxSize 900, overlap 150) on the current seed content — re-generate labels with `npx tsx scripts/dev/dump-chunks.ts` if seed docs change. Keyword coverage is a lexical heuristic, not semantic grading: keywords are matched case-insensitively (dashes/whitespace normalized) against the generated answer.

items.question: How do I measure event loop lag in Node.js and what should I alert on?
items.expectedAnswer: Measure event loop lag with a probe (e.g. an hrtime-based setInterval timer comparing expected vs actual tick time, exported as a Prometheus gauge such as nodejs_eventloop_lag). Sustained lag above ~100 ms means something is monopolizing the loop; alert with a warning at 100 ms and a critical alert at 1 s. After fixes, lag should stay under ~50 ms at peak.

items.question: What pool size should I configure for a small managed Postgres instance running several app processes?
items.expectedAnswer: For a small managed instance a pool max of 5-10 per process is usually plenty; the total across all processes must stay under the provider's connection cap, leaving headroom for migrations and admin sessions. For many processes, route short queries through a transaction-mode pooler (e.g. Supabase Supavisor port 6543, PgBouncer).

items.question: How should I size max-old-space-size for a Node.js container limited to 512 MB of memory?
items.expectedAnswer: Cap the V8 heap explicitly below the container limit, leaving room for non-heap memory (a common rule: heap at roughly 60-75% of the container limit). For a 512 MB container, set NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=384 and verify with v8.getHeapStatistics() that heap_size_limit is ~384 MB inside the container.

items.question: How do I implement ping pong heartbeats for a ws server and configure proxy_read_timeout for WebSocket routes?
items.expectedAnswer: Server sends pings every 25-30 s (browsers cannot ping, but answer with pong frames automatically): track isAlive per client, ping on an interval, and terminate clients that missed a pong. In Nginx, set proxy_http_version 1.1, pass Upgrade/Connection headers, disable buffering, and raise proxy_read_timeout (and proxy_send_timeout) to e.g. 300 s — above heartbeat interval times two, so heartbeats keep it from ever firing.

items.question: How do I prevent a cache stampede when a hot Redis key expires?
items.expectedAnswer: Use a short lock (SET lock:key 1 EX 5 NX) so a single request rebuilds the hot key while others wait briefly and retry the read. Combine with slightly randomized TTLs so cohorts of keys don't expire together, and optionally stale-while-revalidate (serve the stale value while rebuilding in the background).

items.question: Every time our Node service generates a large JSON report it stops answering requests and a single CPU core is pegged at 100%. What is the likely cause and how do we fix it?
items.expectedAnswer: The event loop is being blocked by CPU-bound work (e.g. JSON.parse/stringify on multi-MB payloads). Move the work off the event loop with worker_threads, replace sync calls with async equivalents, paginate/bound the work, and yield in long loops with setImmediate so I/O can drain.

items.question: Two background jobs update the same rows and Postgres randomly kills one of them with a 500; the log hints at a lock cycle. What is the root cause and the fix?
items.expectedAnswer: A deadlock: the two transactions take row locks on the same rows in different orders, so Postgres detects the cycle and rolls one back. Fix by imposing a global lock order (sort ids before updating, or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in sorted order), keeping transactions short, and retrying on SQLSTATE 40P01 with jittered backoff.

items.question: Users keep getting logged out because sessions disappear and our Redis box is at its memory ceiling. What is happening and what should we change?
items.expectedAnswer: Redis hit maxmemory and is evicting keys (evicted_keys climbing). Set an explicit policy for a cache tier — maxmemory at ~70-80% of instance RAM with maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru — and give every cache key a TTL so unbounded growth stops.

items.question: Our Node pod restarts every few days with exit status 137 and there is nothing unusual in the application logs. Where should we look?
items.expectedAnswer: Exit 137 = 128 + SIGKILL: the kernel OOM killer killed the container because the cgroup memory limit was lower than what the Node heap wanted (Node sizes its old-space from host memory by default). Check docker stats / cgroup memory.max vs v8 heap_size_limit, then cap the heap with --max-old-space-size below the container limit.

items.question: Clients with live connections through our reverse proxy get cut at almost exactly the one minute mark, even though the upgrade handshake succeeds with a 101.
items.expectedAnswer: An idle-timeout in the proxy chain is reaping quiet sockets — most often proxy_read_timeout (default 60 s), since WebSockets have no built-in keepalive. Fix with server-side ping/pong heartbeats every 25-30 s to keep frames flowing below every timeout, and raise proxy_read_timeout for the WebSocket location (e.g. 300 s).

items.question: Postgres logs show 'ERROR: deadlock detected (SQLSTATE 40P01)' and some write requests fail with 500. What causes this and how do I fix it?
items.expectedAnswer: Two transactions took row locks on the same rows in different orders, so Postgres detected the lock cycle and killed one (SQLSTATE 40P01). Fix: impose a global lock order (sort ids, or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in sorted order first), keep transactions short, and retry on 40P01 with jittered backoff.

items.question: We keep getting 'ERROR: too many clients already (SQLSTATE 53300)' from PostgreSQL. How do I find out who is holding the connections?
items.expectedAnswer: The app's connection pool is exhausted. Inspect pg_stat_activity (count by state and application_name; look for hundreds of idle connections or idle-in-transaction sessions pointing at leaks). Fix by sizing pools realistically (max 5-10 per process, under the provider cap), always releasing clients in a finally block, and adding acquire timeouts plus pool metrics; use a transaction-mode pooler for many processes.

items.question: Redis writes fail with "OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'" — what should we configure?
items.expectedAnswer: Redis hit maxmemory with policy noeviction, so writes are rejected. For a pure cache set maxmemory to ~70-80% of instance RAM and maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru (or volatile-lru), and give every cache key a TTL. Diagnose with redis-cli INFO memory / --bigkeys.

items.question: Nginx logs 'upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out) while reading response header from upstream' and returns 502s. How do I fix it?
items.expectedAnswer: The upstream endpoint is slower than proxy_read_timeout (default 60 s), so Nginx gives up while reading the response header. Set proxy_read_timeout above the app's true worst-case p99, fix the slow upstream (often event-loop blocking or pool exhaustion), enable upstream keepalive with proxy_http_version 1.1 and an empty Connection header, and retry idempotent requests with proxy_next_upstream.

items.question: Nginx error log shows 'upstream prematurely closed connection' — what does it mean and how do I stop it?
items.expectedAnswer: The upstream closed the connection mid-response — usually idle keepalive connections closed by the app sooner than Nginx reuses them (e.g. behind a pooler or after an app restart), or the app crashing. Enable upstream keepalive (keepalive 32) with proxy_http_version 1.1 and proxy_set_header Connection "" so Nginx stops reusing dead connections, and make sure the app logs slow requests.

items.question: Nginx intermittently returns 502 for our slow Node.js endpoints, and WebSocket clients behind the same proxy reconnect every 60 seconds. How do we fix both problems?
items.expectedAnswer: Both trace to proxy timeouts. For the 502s: raise proxy_read_timeout above the slowest legitimate endpoint's p99 and fix the slow upstream; enable upstream keepalive (proxy_http_version 1.1, empty Connection header). For the WebSockets: server-side ping/pong heartbeats every 25-30 s keep frames flowing below the idle timeout, plus a dedicated location with Upgrade/Connection headers, proxy_buffering off, and proxy_read_timeout raised (e.g. 300 s).

items.question: Our Node upstream behind Nginx becomes unresponsive under load — one CPU core is pinned at 100% while health checks time out — and Nginx starts returning 502s. What should we fix on the app and on the proxy?
items.expectedAnswer: On the app: the event loop is blocked by CPU-bound work — measure event loop lag, profile with node --prof, move work to worker_threads, replace sync calls with async equivalents, and yield in long loops. On the proxy: set proxy_read_timeout above the app's worst-case p99, enable upstream keepalive, and use proxy_next_upstream for idempotent retries so slow endpoints surface as app metrics instead of gateway errors.

items.question: Postgres is falling over under load: we see 'too many clients already' errors while concurrent updates deadlock. How do we stabilize the database?
items.expectedAnswer: Two separate issues. Pool exhaustion (53300): check pg_stat_activity for idle/leaking connections, size pools to 5-10 per process under the provider cap, always release clients in finally, add acquire timeouts, and use a transaction-mode pooler for many processes. Deadlocks (40P01): impose a global row-lock order (sort ids or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in order), keep transactions short — long-held connections inside transactions make both problems worse — and retry on 40P01.
